title: How many hours of education does a mortgage loan originator need under the SAFE Act?
seoTitle: SAFE Act MLO education and CE
description: SAFE Act and 12 CFR 1008 education rules for mortgage loan originators: 20 hours of pre-licensing, 8 hours of annual CE, and the bank registration rules.
shortAnswer: Under the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act (SAFE Act) and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Regulation H (12 CFR Part 1008), a state-licensed mortgage loan originator must complete at least 20 hours of NMLS-approved pre-licensing education, pass a written test with at least 75 percent, and complete at least 8 hours of approved continuing education every year to renew. Registered bank and credit union originators are not subject to these hours.
keyTakeaways: Pre-licensing: at least 20 hours, including 3 hours of federal law and regulations, 3 hours of ethics (fraud, consumer protection and fair lending) and 2 hours on nontraditional mortgage lending standards (12 U.S.C. 5104(c); 12 CFR 1008.105(d)).
Annual continuing education: at least 8 hours, including 3 hours of federal law, 2 hours of ethics and 2 hours on nontraditional mortgage lending (12 U.S.C. 5105(b); 12 CFR 1008.107(a)(2)).
Credit counts only in the year the course is taken, and the same course cannot be repeated in the same or a successive year (12 CFR 1008.107(b)).

Employees of banks, savings associations and credit unions register with the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System and Registry under Regulation G (12 CFR Part 1007) and carry no federal hour requirement, but their employer must instruct them on registration and test compliance at least annually.
States set the minimum and may add more; many add state-specific hours on top of the federal 8, so the state rule always needs checking.
jurisdiction: United States (federal minimum standards, implemented by each state)
regulator: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which administers Regulation G and Regulation H; state mortgage regulators license individuals through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System and Registry (NMLS)
appliesTo: Individuals who take residential mortgage loan applications and offer or negotiate loan terms for compensation, in a state-licensed capacity
Independent contractor loan processors and underwriters, who must be licensed under 12 CFR 1008.103(d)
Nonbank mortgage lenders, brokers and servicers that employ state-licensed originators
Banks, savings associations, credit unions and Farm Credit System institutions, for their registered (not licensed) originators under 12 CFR Part 1007

sections.heading: What does the SAFE Act require of mortgage loan originators?

blocks.text: The SAFE Act requires every individual who originates residential mortgage loans to be either licensed by a state or registered with the national registry, and it sets federal minimum education, testing and background standards for licensing. It was enacted on July 30, 2008 as Title V of the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 and is codified at 12 U.S.C. Chapter 51.

The statute splits originators into two groups. Employees of depository institutions (banks, savings associations, credit unions) become **registered** loan originators under the federal rule in [12 CFR Part 1007](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1007), known as Regulation G. Everyone else, typically employees of independent mortgage companies and brokers, must be **state-licensed** under a state law that meets the minimum standards in [12 CFR Part 1008](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1008), known as Regulation H. The education hours on this page apply to the second group.

An individual is "engaged in the business of a loan originator" under 12 CFR 1008.103(b) if, in a commercial context and habitually or repeatedly, they take a residential mortgage loan application and offer or negotiate loan terms for compensation or gain, or advertise that they can do so. Independent contractors who perform clerical or support duties as loan processors or underwriters must also be licensed under 1008.103(d).

sections.heading: What pre-licensing education and testing is required?

blocks.text: Before a state can issue a license, the applicant must complete at least 20 hours of pre-licensing education approved by the NMLS and pass the national written test with at least 75 percent correct answers. The content split is fixed in the statute at [12 U.S.C. 5104(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title12/html/USCODE-2023-title12-chap51-sec5104.htm) and repeated in [12 CFR 1008.105](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1008/subpart-B/section-1008.105).

blocks.title: 12 CFR 1008.105(d): the pre-licensing minimum
blocks.text: "Completed at least 20 hours of pre-licensing education that has been reviewed and approved by the Nationwide Mortgage Licensing System and Registry. The pre-licensing education completed by the individual must include at least: (1) 3 hours of Federal law and regulations; (2) 3 hours of ethics, which must include instruction on fraud, consumer protection, and fair lending issues; and (3) 2 hours of training on lending standards for the nontraditional mortgage product marketplace."

The remaining 12 of the 20 hours are electives at the federal level, although many states direct some of them to state law. Testing has its own rules in 12 CFR 1008.105(e): a candidate may sit the test three consecutive times with at least 30 days between attempts, and after three failures must wait at least 6 months. A formerly licensed originator who goes 5 years or longer without a valid license, not counting time as a registered originator, must retake and pass the test.

sections.heading: What continuing education is required each year?

blocks.text: A state-licensed originator must complete at least 8 hours of NMLS-approved continuing education each year to be eligible to renew, including 3 hours of federal law and regulations, 2 hours of ethics and 2 hours on nontraditional mortgage lending standards. The rule is in [12 U.S.C. 5105(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title12/html/USCODE-2023-title12-chap51-sec5105.htm) and [12 CFR 1008.107](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1008/subpart-B/section-1008.107).

blocks.text: Three mechanics in 12 CFR 1008.107(b) and (c) shape how training is scheduled. Credit counts only in the year the course is taken, so hours cannot be banked forward. An approved course cannot be repeated in the same year or in successive years to satisfy the requirement, which rules out reusing one annual course. An originator who teaches an approved continuing education course earns 2 hours of credit for every hour taught. Under 12 U.S.C. 5105(b)(5) the NMLS approves courses but may not offer them itself.

sections.heading: Do bank and credit union loan officers need the same hours?

blocks.text: No. Registered originators employed by depository institutions have no federal pre-licensing, testing or continuing education hours, but their employer carries policy and training duties instead. Under [12 CFR 1007.103](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1007/section-1007.103) each such employee must register with the registry, obtain a unique identifier and maintain the registration, and the institution must not let an unregistered employee act as an originator.

[12 CFR 1007.104](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1007/section-1007.104) requires written policies and procedures that, among other things, require all originators to "be informed of the registration requirements of the S.A.F.E. Act and this part and be instructed on how to comply", set up tracking systems to monitor registration and renewal, and provide independent compliance testing "at least annually". This is not a continuing education hour count, but it is a training and evidence obligation an examiner can test. Fair lending and consumer protection training for these staff comes from separate rules, covered in [fair lending and UDAAP training](/regulations/fair-lending-and-udaap-training).

sections.heading: What happens when an originator moves from a bank to a mortgage company?

blocks.text: A registered originator who joins a state-licensed mortgage company can originate under temporary authority while their license application is pending, for up to 120 days if the application stays incomplete. [12 U.S.C. 5117](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title12/html/USCODE-2023-title12-chap51-sec5117.htm) grants this authority to individuals who were registered in the NMLS during the preceding year, have not had a license denied, revoked or suspended, and have applied in the new state. The same section gives temporary authority to licensed originators moving between states.

Temporary authority does not waive the education requirement. The individual still has to complete the 20 hours and pass the test to obtain the license, so employers hiring from banks should plan pre-licensing education into onboarding rather than treating the transition period as a grace period. The [onboarding guide for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles) covers sequencing.

sections.heading: Can states require more than the federal minimum?

blocks.text: Yes. The SAFE Act and Regulation H set minimum standards, and a state can impose additional education, so the federal 20 and 8 hours are a floor rather than the full answer for any individual. Regulation H required states to have compliant requirements in effect no later than August 29, 2011 (12 CFR 1008.109), and the NMLS publishes each state's education requirements for pre-licensing and continuing education.

A multistate originator therefore needs a per-license view: the federal core, plus each state's additional content. Keeping that view current is a refresh-cycle problem as much as a content problem; the method in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) applies. Firms operating across the US can find related obligations on the [financial services industry page](/industries/financial-services) and in the [Bank Secrecy Act AML training](/regulations/bsa-aml-training-requirements) page, which covers the separate AML training that nonbank residential mortgage lenders and originators owe as loan or finance companies under 31 CFR 1029.210.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each SAFE Act and state requirement to the roles and licenses it applies to before any course is chosen, so the federal core, state additions and employer obligations under Regulation G sit in one framework. Completion records are then linked to the clause they satisfy, which makes renewal readiness and examination evidence a query rather than a reconciliation exercise.

faqs.q: Can a mortgage loan originator carry extra CE hours into next year?
faqs.a: No. 12 CFR 1008.107(b) requires states to provide that a licensed originator receives credit for a continuing education course only in the year it is taken, and cannot apply credits from one year to meet a later year's requirement. Hours completed beyond the minimum in one year do not reduce the next year's 8 hours.

faqs.q: Can an originator take the same CE course every year?
faqs.a: No. Under 12 U.S.C. 5105(b)(3)(B) and 12 CFR 1008.107(b), an originator may not meet the annual requirement by taking the same approved course in the same year or in successive years. Providers typically release new course versions each year for this reason, and records should show distinct course identifiers year to year.

faqs.q: Do instructors get credit for teaching continuing education?
faqs.a: Yes. A licensed originator who is approved to teach an approved continuing education course receives credit toward their own annual requirement at 2 hours for every 1 hour taught, under 12 U.S.C. 5105(b)(4) and 12 CFR 1008.107(c).

faqs.q: What happens if a licensed originator lets their license lapse?
faqs.a: If a formerly state-licensed originator goes 5 years or longer without a valid license, ignoring any time spent as a registered originator, they must retake the national test and score at least 75 percent under 12 CFR 1008.105(e)(3). Shorter lapses are handled under each state's reinstatement rules, which may require late continuing education.

factCheck.claim: 12 CFR 1008.105(d): at least 20 hours NMLS-approved pre-licensing education including 3 hours federal law and regulations, 3 hours ethics (fraud, consumer protection, fair lending) and 2 hours nontraditional mortgage lending standards.

12 CFR 1008.105(e): test score not less than 75 percent; three consecutive attempts at least 30 days apart, then 6 month wait; retest required after 5 or more years without a valid license, excluding time as a registered originator.

12 CFR 1008.107(a)(2): at least 8 hours annual NMLS-approved CE including 3 hours federal law, 2 hours ethics, 2 hours nontraditional mortgage lending; (b) credit only in year taken, no carry forward, no repeat course in same or successive years; (c) instructor credit 2 hours per hour taught.
12 U.S.C. 5104(c) and 5105(b) set the same 20 hour and 8 hour minimums in statute; 5105(b)(5)(A) bars the NMLS from offering CE courses; enacted by Pub. L. 110-289, July 30, 2008.
12 CFR 1008.103(b) and (d): definition of engaging in the business of a loan originator; independent contractor processors and underwriters must be licensed.

12 CFR 1007.103(a): employees of covered financial institutions acting as MLOs must register with the Registry and obtain a unique identifier; institution must not permit unregistered employees to act as MLOs.
12 CFR 1007.104(b), (e), (f): policies must require MLOs to be informed of registration requirements and instructed how to comply; tracking systems; independent testing at least annually.

12 U.S.C. 5117(b): temporary authority for registered originators moving to state-licensed mortgage companies, ending at the earliest of withdrawal, denial, grant, or 120 days if the application is listed as incomplete; registered in NMLS during the preceding 1 year.
12 CFR 1008.109(a): state requirements effective no later than August 29, 2011.
